name: Chainsaw chaps and chainsaw trousers
summary: Leg protection for chainsaw work: chaps buckled over trousers, or trousers with the pad built in, filled with long fibres that a running chain pulls out and jams into its drive sprocket.
uses: Running any chainsaw: OSHA's logging rule wants cut-resistant leg protection over the full thigh to the top of the boot, and BC requires it for a worker running a chainsaw, firefighters at a structural fire excepted (OSHA 1910.266, WorkSafeBC Part 8)
They guard only where the pad is, and the rating has to suit the saw: each class is tested to a chain speed (STIHL cut protection)
Less sure against electric and battery saws, whose motors keep their torque and can cut on through the fibres; wear them anyway (UW Extension chainsaw)
No clothing gives absolute protection (STIHL UK PPE), and the Forest Service says not to use chaps as a chain stop (USFS chaps care)
identify: Chaps buckle round the legs and waist over ordinary trousers; chainsaw trousers have the pad sewn in. Under the shell is a thick pad: the Forest Service's is five layers of aramid (Kevlar) in coated nylon (USFS chaps care); CCOHS describes pads of ballistic nylon (CCOHS chainsaw PPE). When the chain touches it, it pulls out the long fibres, which wrap round the drive sprocket and stop the saw (STIHL cut protection, USFS chaps care). Labels: STIHL's US chaps are classified by UL as cut-resistant leg protection for petrol-saw users, to the ASTM F1897 standard and the ASTM F1414 test (STIHL chaps guide). European marks are EN ISO 11393 (part 2) or the older EN 381-5, with a class for chain speed: 0, 1, 2 and 3 for up to 16, 20, 24 and 28 m/s; design A, B or C changes which areas carry the pad (STIHL cut protection, WorkSafeBC Part 8, EN 381-5 listing). A Husqvarna 450 II's chain runs at 17.4 m/s at full power, beyond class 0 (Husqvarna 450 II). BC wants a permanent label with the maker, standards and year made (WorkSafeBC Part 8). Forest Service chaps are orange, sized 32, 36 or 40 in long, labelled USDA Forest Service Specification 6170 (USFS 6170-4L). Chainsaw boots carry a white label with a green fir tree (CCOHS footwear); CSA Z195 is the footwear standard (CCOHS chainsaw PPE).
test: Retire chaps whose shell has many holes and cuts (bar oil gets into the pad and glues the fibres), with chips or sawdust inside the bottom layers, a patch stitched through the pad, oil and dirt caked on that won't wash out, or a cut more than 2.5 cm (1 in) long in the first layer of the pad (USFS chaps care). Retire any pair a running chain has cut into: the chain cuts the outer layer and pulls fibres out of the pad (STIHL cut protection, ACES chaps), Alabama Extension says to discard chaps once the protective inside is exposed (ACES chaps), and BC takes leg protection with damage that affects its performance out of service (WorkSafeBC Part 8). Fit: snug, the pad from the thigh to the boot top (OSHA 1910.266), reaching 5 cm (2 in) below the boot tops (USFS chaps care) and not touching the toe (STIHL chaps guide). Wash them as the label says, because makers differ: STIHL Canada's protective clothing goes in the machine at up to 60 °C with a spin of 400 rpm or less, then air dries; STIHL's US chaps machine-wash warm and tumble dry; Forest Service chaps must not be machine washed or dried, only scrubbed, rinsed cold and line dried, and Alabama Extension says never to use a dryer, because heat can damage the material (ACES chaps). With no label, hand-wash and air dry, as the Forest Service and Alabama Extension both do (USFS chaps care, ACES chaps). No bleach in any of them (STIHL cut protection, STIHL chaps guide, USFS chaps care, USFS 6170-4L).

decay.note: Estimate. STIHL UK recommends 1 to 1.5 years of use for protective clothing in professional forestry and up to 5 years for occasional users, and says chainsaw protective clothing ages (STIHL UK PPE). Oil and bleach lower the protection, and pressure washing destroys the pad (USFS chaps care).

improvise: There is no field substitute: the protection is a deep pad of long, loose fibres that jam the sprocket (STIHL cut protection, USFS chaps care), and ordinary trousers have no such pad. Don't stitch through a pad to mend it: stitching stops the fibres moving and lowers the protection (USFS chaps care). Mend holes in the outer shell soon, before sawdust and oil get in, with a flexible, waterproof seam sealer such as Seam Grip: a dot on small holes, and for tears over 1.2 cm (1/2 in) a piece of paper slipped between the shell and the pad first; let it dry at least 12 hours (USFS chaps care). Without chaps, keep both hands on the saw and never cut above shoulder height (Husqvarna 450 II), and use a bow saw for small wood so the chainsaw does less.
